prize_parts.citation: For determining the structure of nitrogenase and its iron-molybdenum cofactor and for elucidating the mechanism of biological nitrogen fixation.

statement.case_for: Nitrogenase is a chemically extreme reaction, reduction of dinitrogen at ambient conditions, carried out by a metal cluster whose structure was unknown for decades. The crystal structures of the Fe and MoFe proteins and the FeMo-cofactor, including the interstitial carbide resolved at atomic resolution, together with the kinetic account of ATP-gated electron delivery, explain in physical terms how electrons and energy are coupled to a very hard substrate. The structural results are firmly reproduced and have been extended by cryo-EM of turnover states. Having heard colleagues' arguments I still rank it first, because it is the one shortlisted candidacy where a decades-old, unambiguous structural discovery meets a mechanism question of fundamental chemical importance, and where the expert-report evidence on the field is deepest. Rees and Einsle carry the structural decisions and Seefeldt the mechanistic and kinetic strand.
statement.case_against: The catalytic mechanism, meaning where and how N2 binds and the order of intermediates, is still debated, so a prize framed around mechanism would be premature; it would have to be framed around structure. Credit is also spread over at least five people (Dean, Ribbe, Rees, Einsle, Seefeldt), and a three-name cut necessarily omits Dean and Ribbe, whose cofactor biosynthesis and biochemical work are substantial. Opening support is low (a single first place and only three rankings), so this is not where the committee currently converges.

responses.point: Chabes ranks nitrogenase last of his list and judges it premature as a mechanism prize because the catalytic mechanism is still debated.
responses.response: I accept that the mechanism of N2 reduction is open and I would not let a citation claim it is solved. But the Nobel standard has not required a closed mechanism; the structure of the cofactor, including the carbide, is an established discovery that changed how the field thinks, and the citation can be written around structure and the framework for the cycle. I disagree that this makes it premature, in contrast to base editing, where the long-term clinical record that you describe as ripe is still being written.

responses.point: Aqvist puts targeted protein degradation first, with Crews, Deshaies and Handa covering both PROTACs and molecular glues, and emphasises that it is a new pharmacological principle with a quantitatively testable chemistry.
responses.response: I agree that induced proximity is a real conceptual advance and that Handa's cereblon work is what explains the glue branch. My reservation is the one several of us noted: there is still no approved degrader that I can confirm, and the PROTAC and glue strands have different discoverers and different mechanisms. Combining them in one three-person prize forces an arbitrary split. If the committee goes this way I would want the expert report to settle whether the citation is for the PROTAC concept alone, and I would then favour Crews, Deshaies and Ciulli over a mixed set.

responses.point: Linke ranks base editing first with Liu alone, arguing that the invention is clean and original, with Komor and Gaudelli as first authors, and puts nanopore sequencing second.
responses.response: I find the Liu-centred attribution convincing and agree that it is the cleanest in the field. My difficulty is separation from the 2020 CRISPR prize and the early stage of clinical evidence; Komor and Gaudelli as trainees would also be an unusual recognition, so a Liu-only prize would be the honest form. On nanopores I disagree that attribution is manageable: Kasianowicz, Branton, Deamer, Bayley and Akeson each have a distinct claim, and I do not see a defensible three-name set.

responses.point: Zou ranks Buchwald and Hartwig C-N coupling first as an enabling method, and also gives nitrogenase fourth place for its structural value, while noting the credit is spread over five people.
responses.response: I share your view that the structural evidence on the FeMo-cofactor is of the first rank, and that the five-person credit is the main difficulty. I would add that the three-name cap is better handled here than for lipid nanoparticles or sequencing, because the structural and mechanistic strands map onto Rees, Einsle and Seefeldt. For C-N coupling I accept the strong two-person attribution, but I ask whether it is a sufficiently distinct achievement after the 2010 cross-coupling prize.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will accept a structure-centred citation for nitrogenase while the catalytic mechanism remains open.
Whether Dean or Ribbe should displace Seefeldt among the three names.
Whether expert reports show base editing is separable from the 2020 CRISPR prize and mature enough, and whether targeted protein degradation is ripe without an approved drug.
statement.conflict_note: I am a colleague of Xiaodong Zou at Stockholm University, which is a general institutional connection but not a conflict for any shortlisted candidate. Nitrogenase is a metalloenzyme and electron-transfer field adjacent to my own work, but I have no collaboration or personal connection with the candidates, so no specific recusal issue is apparent from the provided profile.
